state.misconception_label: Thinks alternate angles are always equal

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are arguing about alternate angles. Tom says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are alternate. Katie says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are equal. Who is correct? ![Shows two non parallel lines that are intersected by another line. Angles P and Q are both on the outside of the lines and on opposite sides of the transversal.](). I got Only
Katie because I assumed all the angles in the figure are equal.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Actually, in this case, alternate angles are not always equal. Alternate angles are formed when a transversal intersects two parallel lines, not just any intersecting lines. So, in the scenario you provided with Tom and Katie, both Tom and Katie are incorrect because angles \( p \) and \( q \) are not alternate angles. It's important to remember the specific conditions for alternate angles to be equal.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh, I see! So alternate angles are only equal when the lines are parallel. But what if the lines are not parallel? Do they still have any special relationship, or are they just random angles?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: That's correct! When the lines are not parallel, the angles formed are not alternate angles. Instead, they have a different relationship called vertically opposite angles. Vertically opposite angles are always equal, regardless of whether the lines are parallel or not. It's important to distinguish between these different angle relationships when analyzing geometric figures.
